1. The idea in one minute

The problem. OCR (reading text from images) works well on clean scans and badly on damaged documents: faded ink, ink from the back of the page showing through, stains, dark parchment. Damaged documents are also exactly where nobody has typed out (“labelled”) much text to train on.

The usual fix: self-supervised learning (SSL). Let the model practise on unlabelled lines first: hide or damage part of a line and make the model rebuild the clean line (this is a masked autoencoder, MAE). To rebuild it, the model must learn what letters look like and what to ignore. Then a few labelled lines are enough to teach it to output text.

The gap. What damage you add during that practice decides what the model learns to ignore. Today people pick it by hand (“some blur, some noise”). We measure the damage on real old pages, build damage models that match those measurements, and practise with that. Then we test (1) whether it helps, (2) on what kinds of new data it still helps, and (3) whether “how much the model ignores damage X” predicts “how much damage X hurts its accuracy”.

4. Why a pilot, and its four questions

You asked whether this project is worth pursuing. The project rests on four bets. If any of the first three is false, the plan needs changing. Each has a pass rule written down before seeing results, so the answer can’t be bent afterwards.

#The betTestPass if…Now
A1Damage really hurts recognitionTrain on clean IAM, test with 7 damage types × 3 strengths; also real damaged linesError at least doubles for ≥ 2 damage types at medium strengthruns after baseline
A2Real old lines differ measurably from clean ones8 statistics, IAM vs CATMuS≥ 3 damage statistics clearly separated (KS D ≥ 0.5)first pass invalid; redoing
A3Pretraining helps with few labels, at our small scaleSame encoder: from scratch vs MAE-pretrained, 2 seedsPretrained beats scratch by more than the seed-to-seed spread somewheretonight
A4Derived damage ≥ hand-picked damageMAE + derived vs MAE + hand-pickedDerived error ≤ hand-picked (only a hint after one week)tonight

How to read the outcome: A1–A3 pass → go. A3 fails → the main risk from your deck happened (SSL doesn’t beat training from scratch at this scale); pivot to the analysis part (RQ3), which is a result either way. A1 or A2 fails → the motivation is weak; rethink. A4 is too early to decide anything; it is a hint for Phase II.

Measuring real damage: first pass (contaminated, being redone)

Do not quote this figure yet. It was measured before the black-border problem in section 9 was found. The black areas around CATMuS lines were counted as ink, and their edges as faint grey. So “ink fraction”, “stroke width”, “contrast” and especially “faint grey on paper” (the show-through measure, D = 0.93) are inflated. “Paper level” (D = 0.83) is probably still real: parchment is darker. The cleaned data is being measured again tonight, and this figure will be replaced.

What “derived” means, concretely (provisional numbers)

For each damage type, turn its knob up step by step on clean IAM lines and watch the matching statistic move. Then read each real CATMuS line’s statistic back through that curve: “this line looks like show-through at opacity 0.4”. That gives how often each damage occurs and how strong it is. The hand-picked recipe uses the same seven types, each applied half the time at a guessed strength, which is what papers usually do.

8. Literature check (redone today)

  • The key Sep 2026 paper is real and now accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Garrido-Munoz & Calvo-Zaragoza, arXiv 2609.35473; verified on arxiv.org, full text read). On six handwriting datasets, pixel-rebuilding pretraining (MAE) beats contrastive and JEPA methods. Frozen-encoder CER at full labels: MAE 5.5%, SimMIM 8.7%, V-JEPA-2 10.6%, MoCo-v3 19.2%. This supports your choice of MAE.
  • Their augmentation is hand-picked and unspecified: “a fixed augmentation pipeline” of blur, noise, brightness and so on, described only as “small”, “mild” and “low”, with no ranges and no reason. That is your problem statement, inside a NeurIPS paper. Use it in the viva.
  • 2026 sweep: no paper found that derives image damage for text-recognition pretraining from real measurements. Two 2026 papers fit corruption to real data at the text level (simulated OCR typos for post-correction), which is a different problem. New 2026 SSL-for-handwriting papers to cite: LoGo-HTR (WACV), FP-THD (MAE, Jan), WSCL-2HTR.
  • Details and the table are in literature/landscape_2026-11-09.md, section 4b. (“Not found” is not “proven absent.”)

9. Problems caught today (and why they matter)

CATMuS lines come with black borders. Each line is cut out of the page along its outline and everything outside is painted pure black (99% of lines, about 15% of each image). The measurements read that as ink and as faint grey edges, so the first comparison overstated how different the manuscripts are. Fix: the black area is replaced by the local paper colour, and measurements now use only real pixels (a stored mask). All CATMuS data is being rebuilt.

Each group: original line (black border) → cleaned line → mask of real pixels (white). Castilian lines from the first inspection.

The ViT gave different answers depending on its batch-mates. Without a padding mask, a short line read next to a long one was “seeing” the blank padding. The same line gave different outputs (difference 0.92); after the fix, 0.000001. Every pretraining comparison uses this model, so this would have silently corrupted the main results.

Training was idling. A GPU auto-tuning setting re-tuned itself for every new line width; switched off, training runs at about 8 steps per second.

11. The end goal

Short term (17 Nov): show the panel the gap is real and current, the data and compute are feasible (it already runs), and the first results, including the honest ones that didn’t work.

Phase II (Jan–May 2027): proper physical damage models fitted per type, a few hundred real lines tagged by damage type, all five models with more seeds → answer RQ1 and RQ2.

Phase III (Jun–Dec 2027): the invariance-vs-error analysis (RQ3, the H3 sign flip), new scripts (Indic, Arabic), ablations → a workshop paper (ICDAR), then a full paper; release the code, the fitted damage settings and the tagged lines.

What makes it a paper either way: if derived damage wins, that is the method. If it doesn’t, “which damage should a model ignore, and can we predict it?” (RQ3) is still a finding.

13. Words used here

CERCharacter error rate: edits needed to turn the model’s output into the true text, divided by the true text’s length.
SSLSelf-supervised learning: learning from unlabelled data by solving a made-up task (here: rebuild the clean line).
MAEMasked autoencoder: hide 75% of the image patches and rebuild them. “Derived MAE” also damages the visible part and asks for the clean version.
CRNN, CTCClassic line reader: convolutions → a bidirectional LSTM → CTC, the loss that lets a model output text without knowing where each letter is.
ViTVision transformer: cuts the line into 16×8-pixel patches and lets them attend to each other. This is what MAE pretrains (6.5M parameters).
Fine-tune, label budgetAfter pretraining, train on a few labelled lines; 1% of IAM is 65 lines.
Seed spreadThe same run with a different random seed gives a slightly different score; a “win” smaller than that spread means nothing.
Invariance scoreHow similar the model’s internal features are for a clean line and its damaged copy (1 = it ignores that damage completely).
KS DHow different two distributions are, from 0 (identical) to 1 (no overlap).
Held-out damageA damage type never shown during pretraining, used only at test time to see what transfers.
